content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 9: Input Validation, Output Encoding, and Injection Fundamentals. It builds practical understanding of Input Validation with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Input Validation addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Input Validation can be understood through this sequence: Identify input or identity → Apply server-side check → Handle failure safely → Add regression test. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 64.1 Syntactic and semantic validation; 64.2 Allowlist-based validation; 64.3 Type, length, format, and range constraints; 64.4 Server-side validation; 64.5 Validation failures and error handling. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Input Validation
content_blocks.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ContactRequest(BaseModel):
    email: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=254)
    message: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=2000)
content_blocks.expected_output: A valid request is limited by the declared length constraints; invalid input is rejected during model validation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative Pydantic v2 snippet. Install a compatible Pydantic version in a local environment before running it; add semantic email validation appropriate to the product.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Input Validation”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Input Validation in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Input Validation is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
